what_its_for: Alosetron is used to treat severe diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome (IBS-D) in women who have had symptoms for 6 months or more and have not gotten better with other treatments. It works by slowing down the movement of stool through your bowels and reducing belly pain and urgency (the sudden, strong need to go to the bathroom).
how_to_take: Take alosetron by mouth with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Take it at the same time each day to help you remember. Do NOT take more than your doctor prescribed. This medicine is only available through a special program called the Prometheus Prescribing Program for Lotronex — your doctor must be enrolled in this program to prescribe it for you.
dosing: The usual starting dose is 0.5 mg taken twice a day (once in the morning and once in the evening) for the first 4 weeks. If your symptoms are not well controlled after 4 weeks, your doctor may increase your dose to 1 mg twice a day. If your symptoms are still not better after 4 more weeks at the higher dose, you should stop taking this medicine — it may not be right for you.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regularly scheduled time. Do NOT take two doses at the same time or extra doses to make up for the one you missed.
storage: Store alosetron at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep this medicine out of the reach of children. Do not use it after the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking fluvoxamine (an antidepressant) while using alosetron — this combination can cause dangerous levels of alosetron to build up in your body. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines you take, including herbal products. Avoid starting alosetron if you have constipation, bowel blockage, severe liver disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or diverticulitis. Stop taking alosetron and call your doctor right away if you become constipated — do not try to treat constipation on your own while taking this medicine. Avoid smoking if possible, as it may reduce how well alosetron works.
when_to_call_doctor: Stop taking alosetron and call your doctor or go to the emergency room RIGHT AWAY if you experience: new or worsening constipation, severe stomach pain or cramping, blood in your stool or rectal bleeding, sudden or worsening stomach pain especially after eating, nausea, vomiting, or fever. These could be signs of a rare but serious condition called ischemic colitis (reduced blood flow to the bowel) or serious complications of constipation. Also call your doctor if your IBS symptoms are not improving after 4 weeks of treatment.
when_it_works: Some people notice improvement in their IBS symptoms (such as less urgency, fewer trips to the bathroom, and less belly pain) within the first few weeks of treatment. If you do not feel better after 4 weeks at your starting dose, your doctor may adjust your dose. If you still do not feel better after another 4 weeks, talk with your doctor about stopping the medicine.
special_populations: Alosetron is approved ONLY for women with severe diarrhea-predominant IBS — it has not been shown to be effective in men. It has not been studied in children and is not recommended for use in patients under 18 years of age. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor before taking alosetron, as the safety during pregnancy is not fully known. It is not known if alosetron passes into breast milk, so discuss breastfeeding with your doctor. If you have liver problems, use with caution and talk to your doctor, as alosetron is processed by the liver.
